opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things I'm most excited about. When you train a large model on DNA, like a genomic foundation model, it learns to predict sequences really well. And to do that well, it almost has to build some internal representation of the underlying biology: where genes start and stop, what regulatory elements look like, maybe even structural features of the proteins that get encoded. But all of that is locked up inside the model's weights and activations. We can't read it.

Unsupervised interpretability techniques, things like sparse autoencoders, let us decompose those internal representations into features without telling the model in advance what we're looking for. That's the key part. With supervised probing, you can only find concepts you already know to ask about. With unsupervised methods, the model can surface concepts on its own terms.

So the first thing we hope for is validation. You open up the model and find features that line up with things biologists already know: exon-intron boundaries, transcription factor binding motifs, protein secondary structure, even things like mobile genetic elements or viral sequences. That tells you the model has learned real biology rather than superficial statistical tricks.

But the really exciting part is the features that don't map onto anything we have a name for yet. If the model has picked up on some pattern in the genome that's predictive and consistent but that humans haven't characterized, that's potentially a new biological concept. The model becomes a kind of microscope. Instead of us looking directly at the DNA, we're looking at what the model learned from billions of base pairs, which is far more than any human could ever read.

Longer term, I think this changes how science gets done. You go from training a model, getting predictions, and trusting a black box, to training a model and then asking it, "What did you learn?" Then you take those hypotheses into the lab. If even a handful of those features turn out to be real, previously unknown biology, that's a whole new way of making discoveries. Interpretability stops being just a safety or debugging tool and becomes a discovery engine.

r001.rationale: The response describes finding known and previously unknown genomic patterns, but it does not identify uncovering biological functions in DNA considered “junk” as a possible benefit.

fable-5.1.text:
That's the question I get most excited about, honestly. The thing to understand about the genome is that we've been reading it for twenty-five years and we still don't understand most of it. Something like ninety-eight percent of human DNA doesn't code for proteins, and for a long time we called that "junk," which was really just a confession that we didn't know what it was doing.

So what I hope unsupervised methods can do is let the data tell us what matters, rather than us telling the model what to look for. The reason that's such a big deal is that every supervised approach we've had in genomics is bottlenecked by labels, and labels come from experiments, and experiments are slow and expensive and biased toward the things we already suspected were interesting. If you train a model to predict "is this a gene," you'll get something good at finding genes. You won't discover the thing nobody had a name for yet.

When you instead take a very large model and ask it simply to learn the statistics of sequence, to predict what comes next across billions of base pairs and across millions of species, something interesting happens. The model has to build an internal representation of the grammar of DNA to do that well. It has to figure out that certain motifs co-occur, that there's structure at the scale of a few bases and structure at the scale of tens of thousands, that some regions are under intense pressure from evolution and others can drift freely. None of that was in a label. It fell out of the compression problem.

What I'm hoping those representations reveal, concretely, is a few things. One is regulatory logic: how the non-coding regions actually decide when and where a gene turns on, which is where most of the variation that affects disease lives. Two is function for the huge number of genes we can name but can't explain. There are thousands of human proteins where we know the sequence and have essentially no idea what they do. And three, and this is the more speculative one, is evolutionary constraint we haven't noticed. If a model trained purely on sequence consistently treats a region as low-entropy, as something it can confidently predict, that's a signal that biology cares about that region, even if no experiment has ever flagged it.

The honest caveat is that an embedding is not an explanation. The model can tell you two sequences are similar in some learned sense, and then you still have to go into the lab and find out why. I think of these models less as oracles and more as hypothesis generators that are much better calibrated than our intuitions. They narrow the search from the entire genome down to the hundred places worth looking. That alone changes the economics of discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says unsupervised methods could reveal what non-coding DNA—long called “junk”—does, including how it regulates when and where genes turn on.

astra-6.text: What I hope is that they can help us discover patterns in DNA that we don’t yet know to look for. We can read the sequence, but understanding how that sequence controls what happens in a cell is a much harder problem. Unsupervised learning gives us a way to look for structure without first having to label what every piece does. Maybe that reveals relationships between distant regions, or clues about how genes are regulated. Those patterns would still need experimental validation, but they could give us new hypotheses—and ultimately help us understand how changes in DNA lead to changes in biology.

r001.rationale: The response describes finding unknown DNA patterns and clues about gene regulation, but it does not identify uncovering biological functions in DNA considered “junk” as a possible benefit.

sol-6.1.text: What excites me is the possibility of learning the language of DNA without having to tell the model in advance what to look for. We know how to read the sequence, but there’s still so much we don’t understand about how it works. Unsupervised techniques could uncover patterns that help us understand how genes are regulated, how different parts of the genome interact, and which variations might matter. Ideally, those patterns would give us new hypotheses that we can then test experimentally.

r001.rationale: The response mentions discovering patterns in DNA, including gene regulation and genome interactions, but does not identify uncovering biological functions in DNA considered “junk” as a possible benefit.
